solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: No saint, unscrupulous individual is filled with constant agitation (9)

indicatorNotes.No: 'No saint' asks for a word with the saint taken out: the S that stands for saint is refused entry.
indicatorNotes.is filled with: Something filled with a thing has it inside, so IS wraps round the letter that follows.

blocks.note: SHYSTER (an unscrupulous individual) without S = saint
used as is
c = a constant, as in the speed of light; sits inside IS

annotation.surface: A moralist frets about some villain who is anything but saintly.
annotation.walkthrough: A shyster is a crook, especially a dishonest lawyer. 'Constant' reads as a steady adjective in the surface but is the physicist's symbol.
annotation.definitionFit: The answer is a noun for a fit of uncontrolled emotional excitement, a plain synonym of agitation in its frantic sense.

entries.clue: Veil what KLM’s after with BA on the rise? (5)

indicatorNotes.on the rise: Something on the rise is going up, and in a down entry going up means the letters read from bottom to top.

blocks.note: in the alphabet K, L, M come straight after H, I, J
BA written upwards

annotation.surface: Two airlines, KLM and British Airways, seem to be jostling over a veil.
annotation.walkthrough: KLM and BA look like airlines, Dutch and British. Here KLM is just three consecutive letters of the alphabet, and 'what it is after' is the three before it.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the answer is the headscarf or veil worn by some Muslim women.

entries.clue: Deputy with very brief experience at the higher level? (6-2-7)

annotation.definition2: very brief experience at the higher level?

blocks.note: the straight sense: the officer just below the leader

blocks.clueFragment: very brief experience at the higher level?
blocks.note: a whimsical reading: one tick of the clock spent in charge

annotation.surface: A deputy gets a fleeting taste of the top job.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the joke: split the answer as 'a second in command' and it becomes a moment's spell at the top.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses: the straight one is the rank just below the leader, the cryptic one reads a second of time spent in command.

entries.clue: Finally lose weight — room for eating dessert? (4,4)

indicatorNotes.Finally: What comes finally comes at the end, so take only the last letter of the word that follows.

blocks.note: last letter of lose
a ton is a weight
a mess is the room where military personnel eat

annotation.surface: A dieter needs to lose weight, but is there still room for pudding?
annotation.walkthrough: Eton mess is a British dessert of crushed meringue, strawberries and cream, named after Eton College. The question mark admits it is only one example of a dessert.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the answer is one particular British pudding, hence the question mark after dessert.

entries.clue: Religious figure present in anima mundi (4)

indicatorNotes.present in: Something present in a phrase is already there among its letters, waiting to be spotted across the word break.

blocks.note: anIMA Mundi

annotation.surface: A mystic claims a holy figure dwells in the world soul.
annotation.walkthrough: Anima mundi is Latin for the soul of the world, which suits a religious surface and hides the join between the two words.
annotation.definitionFit: The answer leads prayers in a mosque, so a religious figure is a fair general description.

entries.clue: Talk of flogging tar after beer stashed in ship (5,5)

indicatorNotes.stashed in: Goods stashed in a hold are hidden inside it, so the beer goes inside the ship.
indicatorNotes.after: One thing coming after another is placed second, so the tar follows the ship-and-beer part.

blocks.note: SS = steamship
ale is beer; it goes inside SS
pitch is tar

annotation.surface: Sailors of old talk of flogging and tar, with beer stowed below decks.
annotation.walkthrough: Flogging here is British slang for selling, not whipping, which the naval surface pushes hard.
annotation.definitionFit: British slang: flogging means selling, and the answer is the patter a seller uses.

entries.clue: Volume dial adjusted for sound (5)

indicatorNotes.adjusted: Something adjusted has been altered and set differently, so the letters of the word before it are rearranged.

blocks.note: v = volume
DIAL rearranged

annotation.surface: Someone twiddles the volume knob on a stereo.
annotation.walkthrough: With volume and dial in play, 'sound' looks like noise; it is the adjective meaning well-founded.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the adjective sense: a well-founded argument is both sound and logically acceptable.

entries.clue: Truth the ne plus ultra really involves (6)

indicatorNotes.involves: A thing that involves another takes it in as part of itself, so the word for really wraps round the one for the ultimate.

blocks.note: very = really, as in 'very good'
'it' is the ultimate, the thing everyone wants; goes inside VERY

annotation.surface: A philosopher insists the ultimate in anything must involve truth.
annotation.walkthrough: Ne plus ultra is Latin for the highest point attainable; being 'it' carries the same sense.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the answer is a formal, slightly literary word for truth.

entries.clue: Palace women win — good Italian side thrashed (6-2-7)

indicatorNotes.thrashed: Something thrashed is beaten about violently, so the letters are knocked out of order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder
g = good
anagram fodder

annotation.surface: A women's team from the palace beats an Italian side.
annotation.walkthrough: The football surface makes 'thrashed' look like the result; it is the instruction to rearrange everything after 'women'.
annotation.definitionFit: The answer names the women who attend a queen or princess, so they are literally women of the palace.

entries.clue: Person belonging to underworld apparently cut to pieces (9)

blocks.note: Dis is the Roman god of the underworld, and the underworld itself
a member is a person belonging to a group

annotation.surface: A gangster from the criminal underworld seems to have been hacked apart.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Apparently' concedes that the split is a playful misreading, not real etymology: the dis- is really a prefix of separation.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to cut a body to pieces is to tear it limb from limb.

entries.clue: One handy face card turning up in every deal? (4-2-3-6)

blocks.note: the jack is a face card
a trade is a deal, so 'of all trades' = in every deal

annotation.surface: A card player notices the same face card appearing in every hand dealt.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Deal' works twice: dealing cards in the surface, a trade in the wordplay. The question mark flags that playful split.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: the phrase describes a handy person who can turn their hand to any job.

entries.clue: Dull university medic on Scots peak (6)

indicatorNotes.on: In an across clue one thing placed on another comes after it, so the university medic is written after the peak.

blocks.note: ben is Scots for a mountain, as in Ben Nevis
u = university
MB = Bachelor of Medicine, a doctor's degree

annotation.surface: A tedious university doctor sits on a Scottish mountain.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dull' looks like an adjective describing the medic, but it is the verb, to deaden.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the verb sense: to deaden feeling or sensation.

entries.clue: In some way wonder about retaining seat (2,2,4)

indicatorNotes.retaining: Something retaining a thing holds on to it inside, so the word for wonder keeps the seat within it.

blocks.note: awe is wonder
to seat is to sit; goes inside AWE
re = about, concerning

annotation.surface: An MP facing an election wonders whether they will hold their seat.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a parliamentary seat, but the wordplay wants the verb. 'About' tempts as a reversal indicator; it is a piece of its own.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: the phrase hedges a description, meaning so to speak or in a manner of speaking.

entries.clue: Dish Keats cooked — one eaten by Hamlet? (5,5)

indicatorNotes.cooked: Food that is cooked is changed from its raw state, so the poet's letters are rearranged.
indicatorNotes.eaten by: What is eaten by someone ends up inside them, so one goes inside the Dane.

blocks.note: KEATS rearranged
Hamlet is the Prince of Denmark, a Dane
I = one, goes inside DANE

annotation.surface: Two literary heroes in the kitchen: the poet Keats cooks, and Hamlet eats.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark admits Hamlet is only one of many Danes.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by genus: the answer is a pan-fried steak in a creamy sauce, served as a restaurant dish.

entries.clue: Shrub put in particular island area (10)

indicatorNotes.in: One thing put in another sits inside it, so the word for put goes inside the word for particular.

blocks.note: a point is a particular, a detail
to put is to set; goes inside POINT
I = island
a = area

annotation.surface: A gardener plants a shrub in a certain spot on an island.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Particular' is the noun, a detail or point, not the adjective the surface suggests.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by genus: the answer is a Mexican shrub with red bracts, popular at Christmas.

entries.clue: Such breaches as occasion escape from Tyre? (9)

annotation.definition: Such breaches as occasion escape from Tyre?

blocks.note: the surface pushes breaches in city walls that let a besieged population flee; the setter means holes that let something out
the capital hides a car tyre, and what escapes from it is air

annotation.surface: Breaches in a city wall let the people flee the ancient city of Tyre.
annotation.walkthrough: Tyre is the ancient Phoenician city besieged by Alexander, so 'breaches' look military. The capital T hides a car tyre, spelt the British way.
annotation.definitionFit: Read literally, the clue describes holes that let air escape from a car tyre.

entries.clue: Ascend, lopping first branch (4)

indicatorNotes.lopping first: To lop is to cut off a branch, and lopping first cuts off the word's first letter.

blocks.note: CLIMB minus its first letter C

annotation.surface: A tree surgeon climbs up and lops off the lowest branch.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lopping' is a tree surgeon's word, which suits a branch and hides the letter removal.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a large bough of a tree is also called by the word for an arm or leg.

entries.clue: Frame and beds sent north in strengthened vehicle (5,3)

indicatorNotes.sent north: Something sent north travels upwards, and in a down entry that means the letters read from bottom to top.

blocks.note: a rack is a frame
cots are beds; this and the frame are then reversed together

annotation.surface: A bed frame and mattresses are shipped north in a reinforced van.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole of frame-plus-beds is reversed as one string, not each piece separately.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the answer is an ordinary car reinforced for racing and crashing.

entries.clue: Amorously kiss head-turner? (4)

blocks.note: informal verb for kissing and cuddling
the part of the body that literally swivels your head

annotation.surface: Someone gorgeous enough to turn heads gets a passionate kiss.
annotation.walkthrough: A head-turner is normally an attractive person; the question mark signals the literal anatomical reading.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses: the informal verb for kissing and cuddling, and the body part that swivels the head.

entries.clue: Barbican church away from East in flood (10)

indicatorNotes.in: Things placed in a flood are surrounded by it, so church and the westward direction go inside the word for flood.

blocks.note: ch = church
heading away from east is going to W, west
flood water; the church and direction go inside, between T and E

annotation.surface: A church in the Barbican area of London stands away to the east, amid floodwater.
annotation.walkthrough: The Barbican is a London arts centre, but a barbican is a fortified outer gate or tower. 'Away from East' is a direction, to the west.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym from castle-building: a barbican is an outer defensive tower from which guards keep a lookout.

entries.clue: Flock on water doubly good in force 8 (6)

indicatorNotes.in: Something caught in a storm is inside it, so the doubled good goes inside the force 8 wind.

blocks.note: force 8 on the Beaufort wind scale is a gale
g = good, twice; goes inside GALE

annotation.surface: Birds bob on the water, well sheltered, in a severe gale.
annotation.walkthrough: The Beaufort scale runs from 0 (calm) to 12 (hurricane); force 8 is the one named for a strong wind.
annotation.definitionFit: A collective noun: the answer is the word for a flock of geese, birds often seen on water.

entries.clue: Actor, male, scarcely dropping line (3,5)

indicatorNotes.dropping: To drop something is to let it go, so the letter standing for line falls out of the word.

blocks.note: a tom is a male cat
HARDLY (scarcely) minus L = line

annotation.surface: An actor on stage barely manages before forgetting a line.
annotation.walkthrough: Dropping a line is an actor's nightmare, so the surface hides the deletion in theatre talk.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the answer is an English film actor, known for Mad Max: Fury Road.

entries.clue: Cold hearts in MI6: boss there in breach (6)

indicatorNotes.in: Agents in MI6 are inside the organisation, so the cold and hearts letters go inside its initials.

blocks.note: MI6 is the Secret Intelligence Service, SIS
c = cold, as on a tap; goes inside SIS
h = hearts, the card suit; goes inside SIS after C
M is the head of MI6 in the James Bond stories

annotation.surface: A cold-hearted spymaster at MI6 presides over a rift in the service.
annotation.walkthrough: MI6 is the British foreign intelligence agency, formally the Secret Intelligence Service. 'Cold hearts' reads as callousness but is two separate abbreviations.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a split or rupture within a group, especially a church, is a breach.

entries.clue: Crew set about hauling in new painter (5)

indicatorNotes.set about: To set something about is to turn it round, so the crew's letters are written backwards.
indicatorNotes.hauling in: Hauling something in pulls it inside, so the turned-round crew takes the letter for new within it.

blocks.note: a crew is a team; turned about it gives MAET
n = new; sits between the second and third letters of MAET

annotation.surface: A ship's crew hauls a novice painter aboard.
annotation.walkthrough: The sailing surface makes 'hauling' physical; it is the container instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the answer is the French painter Édouard, a forerunner of Impressionism.

entries.clue: Woodcutter’s commercials on radio (4)

indicatorNotes.on radio: What is on radio can only be heard, so the answer is a word that sounds like the commercials.

blocks.note: ads are commercials

annotation.surface: A lumberjack appears in radio advertisements.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Woodcutter's' reads as possessive, but it is 'woodcutter is': the woodcutter is a tool, not the lumberjack the surface suggests.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by function: the answer is an axe-like tool for cutting and shaping wood, so it is literally a wood cutter.

entries.clue: Eurocrat excited with a daring defensive strategy (9,6)

indicatorNotes.excited: Something excited is stirred up and agitated, so its letters are shaken into a new order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder
anagram fodder

annotation.surface: An excited Brussels bureaucrat devises a bold defensive plan.
annotation.walkthrough: 'With' sits between the two runs of fodder; 'a daring' is fodder, not a description of the strategy.
annotation.definitionFit: A military idiom: the phrase means a defensive fight by troops at the rear, and figuratively any last-ditch resistance.

entries.clue: Small border plant in wet ground (5)

blocks.note: s = small
an edge is a border

annotation.surface: A gardener sets a little plant along the border of a boggy bed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Border' suggests a flower bed; it simply means an edge.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the answer is a grass-like plant that grows in marshy ground.

entries.clue: Private investigator smart or simple (9)

blocks.note: a private eye is a private investigator
bright = smart, clever

annotation.surface: Is the private detective clever or a simpleton?
annotation.walkthrough: 'Simple' looks like the opposite of smart; it is an old noun for a medicinal herb.
annotation.definitionFit: An old sense: a simple is a medicinal herb, and this small plant was once used to treat the eyes.
